title: Tuga W8 vs W10: 8 Inch or 10 Inch Rugged Windows Tablet?
description: Tuga W8 (8 inch, £629) or W10 (10.1 inch, £649)? £20 apart, so ports, weight and screen size decide it. Who needs Ethernet?
summary: £20 apart and both on Windows 11 Pro: the W8 is 287g lighter with a sharper 1920 x 1200 screen, MIL-STD-810G, 4G and GPS built in; the W10 adds a 10.1 inch screen, RJ45 Ethernet and a UHF RFID option.
lede: For anyone settled on Windows 11 Pro and choosing between the two Tuga tablets. The short answer: the £20 price gap decides nothing, so buy the Tuga W8 if the tablet is carried around, and the Tuga W10 if it plugs into network gear with a cable or spends its day on a desk or in a vehicle mount showing diagrams.
verdict: Weight and ports decide this one, not price. The Tuga W8 costs £629 and the Tuga W10 £649, a gap of £20 for two tablets that share Windows 11 Pro, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage and the same accessories. The W10's extra £20 buys a 10.1 inch screen against 8 inch and an RJ45 Ethernet port, in a tablet that weighs 1197g against the W8's 910g. The W8's screen is the sharper of the two at 1920 x 1200 against the W10's 1280 x 800, so the W10 shows the same amount at a larger size rather than more detail. The W10 uses an Intel N100 (up to 3.4GHz) where the W8 has an Intel Celeron N5100.

Pay the £20, and carry the extra 287g, if the job involves a cable. The W10's 100Mbps RJ45 Ethernet port plugs straight into control panels, switches and plant that have never seen Wi-Fi, and the W8 lists no Ethernet port at all. That is the engineer's and commissioning case, and the larger screen helps there too, with a wiring diagram at 10.1 inches. Both tablets have a removable 5000mAh battery, but a spare is not listed among our accessories, so ask before you order if you plan on swapping. The W10 also lists a UHF RFID reader as an option, which the W8 does not.

Do not pay it if the tablet is carried around a site all day, lives in your hands or sits out in the weather, rather than being parked on a desk, in a dock or in a vehicle mount: the W8 is the one to buy, and it is the cheaper one too. Both are sealed to IP65, which covers dust and water jets but not immersion, but the W8 is also listed as MIL-STD-810G with 1.22 metre drops and rated for -20°C to 60°C, where the W10 lists neither. It has 4G LTE and GPS + GLONASS built in, where the W10 lists 4G LTE and GPS as options. For a tablet that goes up ladders and into plant rooms, that list is a strong reason to choose the W8. Our guide to tablets for field engineers goes through both tablets and how to choose between them.
chooseA: You carry it rather than dock it: the W8 is 287g lighter, at 910g against 1197g.

You work outdoors: the W8 lists a 550 nit screen, MIL-STD-810G with 1.22 metre drops and a -20°C to 60°C operating range; the W10 is also IP65 but lists no brightness, MIL-STD rating or operating temperature.
You need a mobile connection and a position fix as standard: 4G LTE and GPS + GLONASS are built into the W8, where the W10 lists 4G LTE and GPS as options.
You want the sharper screen: the W8 is 1920 x 1200, where the W10 is 1280 x 800.
You photograph every job: the W8's rear camera is listed at 8MP against the W10's 5MP, though only the W10's is listed as autofocus.
chooseB: You plug into panels, switches or plant with a cable: the W10 has an RJ45 Ethernet port and the W8 lists none.
You read wiring diagrams, drawings or spreadsheets on a desk or in a vehicle mount: 10.1 inches against 8, at a lower 1280 x 800 resolution than the W8's 1920 x 1200.
You want the faster processor: the W10 has an Intel N100 (up to 3.4GHz), against the W8's Celeron N5100 (up to 2.8GHz).
You tag assets with RFID: the W10 lists an optional UHF RFID reader, and the W8 does not.

faq.q: Is the Tuga W10 worth £20 more than the Tuga W8?
faq.a: Only if the cable or the larger screen matters to you. The W10 costs £649 and the W8 £629, and they share Windows 11 Pro, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, a 5000mAh removable battery, HDMI (Mini HDMI on the W8), USB-C, USB-A and NFC. The W10 adds a 10.1 inch screen, RJ45 Ethernet and the option of a UHF RFID reader, and weighs 1197g against 910g. The W8 keeps 4G LTE and GPS as standard, has the sharper 1920 x 1200 screen against the W10's 1280 x 800, and is rated MIL-STD-810G where the W10 lists no MIL-STD rating. Both are IP65. If you do not need the cable or the screen size, buy the Tuga W8. Both include 12 months of warranty, and the paid 3-Year Warranty is £79 on either.

faq.q: Which is tougher, the Tuga W8 or the Tuga W10?
faq.a: On paper, the W8. Both are sealed to IP65, which covers dust and water jets but not immersion, but the W8 is also listed as MIL-STD-810G with 1.22 metre drops and rated to work from -20°C to 60°C. The W10 lists no MIL-STD rating, no drop height and no operating temperature range. Neither is listed as protected against immersion. The W10's case rests on its ports and larger screen rather than its toughness. Our MIL-STD-810H guide explains what the rating does and does not tell you, including 810G against 810H, and the IP rating guide covers what an IP65 rating means in practice.

faq.q: Does the Tuga W10 have 4G and GPS like the W8?
faq.a: As options, not as standard. The W8 has 4G LTE and GPS + GLONASS built in, alongside Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.0 and NFC. The W10's listed connectivity is dual-band Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.2, NFC and 100Mbps Ethernet, with 4G LTE and GPS listed as options without prices, so the standard W10 is a Wi-Fi and cable tablet; ask us before you order if you need either. If the tablet needs its own mobile connection in the van and a position fix without a phone hotspot, the W8 has both built in. Both tablets fit the Vehicle Mounting Dock (£109) and the 12V DC Car Charger (£26) on the accessories page.

faq.q: Can I get the Tuga W8 or W10 with a barcode scanner?
faq.a: Yes, both. The Tuga W8 with 2D Scanner is £699, £70 more than the standard W8, and the Tuga W10 with 2D Scanner is £729, £80 more than the standard W10, so the scanner versions are £30 apart. Each is sold from the same product page as its base model, the W8 page or the W10 page. The W10 also lists a UHF RFID reader as an option, which the W8 does not, so if you tag pallets or tools with RFID rather than barcodes, the W10 is the one to ask about. For a handful of scans a day, a scanning app using the camera may be enough, and you should check that the app runs on the device before relying on it; our guide to built-in barcode scanners explains 1D, 2D and RFID and when the extra cost pays off.
